content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed to understand dropout by introducing a new concept, weight volume. The authors show that: 1. weight volume can effectively capture the generalization ability; 2. dropout expands the weight volume and thus helps generalization.
content.main_review:
Pros:
- This paper introduces a novel and interesting quantity, weight volume, to capture the generalization ability.
- The  PAC-Bayesian analysis is well suitable in this scenario which gives an insightful characterization of why weight volume can indicate generalization ability.
- The empirical results of replacing dropout with disentangled noise appropriately verify that weight expansion can help generalization.

Concerns:
- The major concern is about the experimental results. The authors showed results on several vision datasets with VGG and AlexNet-like models but didn't report some commonly-used metrics like accuracy. This makes it unclear if the results are reliable. Also, more experiments on other domains, e.g., NLP, are encouraged as dropout is more frequently used in NLP. I'll increase my score if this concern is well addressed.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of using weight volume to capture generalization and explain the effect of dropout is novel and interesting, however, more justification on experimental results is needed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the important problem of answering the question "Why does drop-out help with generalization"? The answer presented in this paper comes in two stages by relating drop-out to weight expansion and weight-expansion to generalization. They show both their claims are theoretically supported and then experimentally validate the findings on various applications that are of interest. Their findings are not entirely theoretical however, as they lead to a new method via weight expansion.
content.main_review:
As mentioned in the summary, the main strength of this paper stems from the importance of studying drop-out theoretically. A theoretical understanding of dropout would serve as a substantial contribution to the machine learning community at large since it expands our impression of how deep learning methods are generalising and can be further improved in practice.

This is evidenced by the comprehensive contribution in this work where a new method for regularization is presented, referred to as weight expansion. While the method is not entirely actionable as a new method, the connection at least theoretically is sufficient to warrant as a novel discovery.

This work discusses all related work that is relevant to the best of my knowledge and compares to the right level of depth against any competing methods or possible explanations of drop-out. 

The level of clarity of this paper should also be commended as they use bold text thematically throughout the paper that makes it clear of the two layers of contributions (weight expansion and generalization) which makes the experiments much easier to read. 

I only had one question that I would like to be clarified regarding the further developments coming from this work that involve the study of drop-out or weight expansion in other areas of machine learning. It seems the paper does not explain completely what kind of future developments would benefit and while it is implied, I believe the paper would benefit if written down and expanded upon in the conclusion section. For example, they may mention that this work paves the way to explore regularization in other areas such as in generative models.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the paper should be accepted for presentation due to the importance of the problem tackled and the exposition between weight expansion and generalization. Therefore I vote for acceptance.

content.title: Reply to the Reviewer w6em
content.comment:
We appreciate the positive comments from the reviewer, and the insightful question about future work. Our response is below, we have also included it in Appendix P, and plan to move this discussion to the main text in the camera-ready version (if accept and have enough space).

**Q: I only had one question that I would like to be clarified regarding the further developments coming from this work that involve the study of drop-out or weight expansion in other areas of machine learning. It seems the paper does not explain completely what kind of future developments would benefit and while it is implied, I believe the paper would benefit if written down and expanded upon in the conclusion section. For example, they may mention that this work paves the way to explore regularization in other areas such as in generative models.**

**A:** In this paper, we introduce 'weight expansion', an intriguing phenomenon that appears whenever dropout is applied during training. 
We have provided both theoretical and empirical arguments, which show that weight expansion is one of the key indicators of the reduced generalization error, and that dropout is effective to obtain weight expansion.

For the next steps, we believe the following few directions are worthy of exploration and research (we also thank Reviewer wW51 for the future work suggestions).

1. First, at the moment, we consider weights as a vector, without taking into consideration the structural information that the weights can be closely coupled according to the structures of the layers. It is interesting to know whether or not weight volume may capture some structural information of network (e.g., convolutional layer). 

2. Second, it will be useful to develop more PAC-Bayesian optimization methods [1,2,3] to help expand weight volume. While the methods in the paper have been shown effective and efficient, they are by no means optimal. It is not hard to see that such optimization problem is highly intractable, so an optimal solution may not be practical. Nevertheless, we believe there are rooms for improvement, and any progress in this direction will be significant for not only the problem in this paper but also other problems that may involve PAC-Bayesian optimization.

3.  Third, activation functions have been argued to have a significant impact on not only the trained models but also the training process, related to the first point, it is interesting to understand how weight volume is related to activation functions (e.g., ReLU, tanh). 

4. Last but not least, it can be a significant topic to study whether the weight volume -- when combined with the PAC-Bayesian adversarial generalization bound [4] -- can provide any guidance to the hot topic of adversarial generalization. 

[1] Letarte, Germain, Guedj, Laviolette. Dichotomize and Generalize: PAC-Bayesian Binary Activated Deep Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2019.

[2] Pérez-Ortiz, Rivasplata, Shawe-Taylor, Szepesvári. Tighter Risk Certificates for Neural Networks. JMLR 2021.

[3] Gintare Karolina Dziugaite and Daniel M. Roy. Computing nonvacuous generalization
bounds for deep (stochastic) neural networks with many more parameters than training
data. UAI, 2017.

[4] Farzan Farnia, Jesse M Zhang, and David Tse.  Generalizable adversarial training via spectral nor-malization.ICLR, 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes the "weight volume" as a new metric for neural network model selection. To compute the weight volume, one should first consider a vector of random variables that take values "around" the weights of the neural network without changing its outputs. Then the weight volume is measured from the normalized determinant of the covariance matrix. The paper shows mathematically that increasing the weight volume decreases a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound, and (2) the dropout method naturally endeavors weight volume expansion. Then, the paper presents two methods for estimating the weight volume of a neural network (which is mandatory as neural networks commonly have a large number of parameters). Finally, extensive experiments show empirically a clear correlation between the introduced metric and the generalization gap of neural networks,
content.main_review:
I enjoyed reading the paper as it is based on a clever idea, and contains several interesting insights (listed in the summary of the paper above). However, the current manuscript has several shortcomings. 

(1) First of all, despite being intuitive, the definition of weight volume in Section 3 is unclear about the very nature of the considered random variable. I understood reading the paragraph "Sampling method' of Section 4 that, given a neural network parametrized by weight W, the random variable takes values "around" W since that the neural network outputs are almost unchanged. The precise random variable considered by the "Laplace approximation" is unclear to me.

(2) The analysis of the weight volume through the PAC-Bayes framework is interesting. However, the authors present the PAC-Bayes literature as there was nothing done in that field between the early results of McAllester (1999) and the neural network approaches of Dziugate & Roy (2017) and Neyshabur et al. (2017). This is problematic for at least two reasons:

A. This disregards important early works that develop ideas reused in the current paper. Importantly, the parametrization of the PAC-Bayes bound using Gaussian distribution has been introduced by Langford and Caruana (2001), Seeger (2002), Langford and Shawe-Taylor (2002) and promoted by many others (e.g., Germain et al., 2009, Parrado-Hernández et al. 2012, Alquier et al. 2016). In this regard, giving the credits to 2017-2021 papers for the classic PAC-Bayes bound of McAllester (Eq 3) and the use of Gaussian distributions (Eq 4) is inadequate.

B.  This prevents the authors from exhibiting relations between previously explored idea and their own. For instance, the idea of "expending the volume" while preserving the predictor output is reminiscent of a strategy used in the simplest linear classification setting; that is, one can multiply the weight vector norm by a constant to obtain tight PAC-Bayes generalization bounds, while preserving the output of a (potentially kernelized) linear classifiers (Langford and Shawe-Taylor 2002, Germain et al., 2009, Parrado-Hernández et al. 2012). Also, Alquier et al. (2016) optimize a PAC-Bayesian bound using a Gaussian posterior with a full covariance matrix.

(3) Beginning with the abstract, the text mentions several times that "weight expansion should be regarded as the cause for the increased generalization capacity". This seems an (enthusiastic) overstatement, as the paper shows a correlation more than causality, and the supplementary material shows that other common regularizers - dropout and batch normalization - do not tend to increase the weight expansion (this is elusively mentioned in the paper). While the paper presents an extensive empirical study exhibiting a link between weight expansion and generalization, it does not explain the mechanisms linking both phenomena. Intuitively, I would guess that the weight expansion metric captures a notion of margin or predictive stability, the latter being the cause of generalization. Similarly, explaining the SVM, I would not say that promoting a small weight vector norm is the cause of its generalization ability; however, a small vector norm translates into a large classification margin, which improves generalization.

(4) While the empirical results are promising, a more fine-grained analysis would help understand better the role of "weight volume". One unanswered question is the effectiveness of the metric depending on the architecture choice: Is it as informative for relu or tanh activations? Is the weight volume capturing the adequacy of CNN layers? Another relevant experiment would be to check if the existing PAC-Bayesian bound optimization procedures for neural networks (e.g., Dziugate & Roy, 2017, Letarte et al., 2019, Pérez-Ortiz 2021) naturally promotes large weight volumes.

 Other comments:
- Figure 1. The procedure to generate plots (b) and (d) needs to be explained.
- Section 4: The sentence "For CIFAR-10, we let $\epsilon=0.05$..." should be deferred in the experiments section.
- Section 4.1: Does the notion of "disentanglement noise" come from the literature? If so, please provide references.
- Table 2 results: The generalization gap (GG) metric needs to be properly defined in the main paper, notably the purpose of $\omega$. It is crucial to interpret the results.

### References
- Alquier, Ridgway, Chopin. On the properties of variational approximations of Gibbs posteriors. JMLR 2016.
- Germain, Lacasse, Laviolette, Marchand. PAC-Bayesian learning of linear classifiers. ICML 2009.
- Langford and Caruana. (Not) Bounding the True Error. NIPS 2001.
-Langford and Shawe-Taylor. PAC-Bayes & Margin. NIPS 2002.
- Letarte, Germain, Guedj, Laviolette. Dichotomize and Generalize: PAC-Bayesian Binary Activated Deep Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2019.
- Parrado-Hernández, Ambroladze, Shawe-Taylor, Sun. PAC-Bayes Bounds with Data Dependent Priors. JMLR 2012.
- Pérez-Ortiz, Rivasplata, Shawe-Taylor, Szepesvári. Tighter Risk Certificates for Neural Networks. JMLR 2021.
- Seeger. PAC-Bayesian Generalisation Error Bounds for Gaussian Process Classification. JMLR 2002.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is based on a clever idea, and contains several interesting insights. However, the current manuscript has several shortcomings.
Notably, the literature review on PAC-Bayes learning is clearly inadequate.

content.title: Feedback
content.comment:
I appreciate the clarifications to the paper, but I would argue that the manuscript could be much stronger following a major rewriting. 

The revised version of the paper is still elusive on the very nature of the considered random variable. Neural network weights are not random variables by definition, so what is $\mathbf{W }$ in definition 3? As I wrote in my initial review, I deduced the meaning of the definition when reading Section 4, but it must be precisely defined. I am under the impression that this is obvious in the authors' minds, so they omit to mention it! Similarly, I guess that the visualization of Figures 1(b)(d) are obtained with t-SNE, but it needs to be stated.

I am moderately satisfied by the added paragraph on PAC-Bayes in the related work section. The point of referring to previous work is not only to please their authors! I still think that the proposed analysis share connections with pre-DNN PAC-Bayes works that should be investigated further by the authors. It would also help to clarify the use of random variables (or distributions) in PAC-Bayes; the revised version claims that Langford & Shawe-Taylor treat the weight as deterministic variables, which is disputable as they consider (prior and posterior) distributions over weights. They made a clear distinction between the stochastic (so-called Gibbs) predictor and its deterministic counterpart. By multiplying the weight vector of a linear classifier, they obtain various stochastic predictors sharing a single deterministic counterpart.

replying_to: Replying to Feedback

content.title: Reply to the Feedback.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. Our answers are as follows.

**Q: Neural network weights are not random variables by definition...**

**A:** First of all, we would like to point out that neural network weights **can be modeled** as random variables, and such modeling has been widely accepted in the deep learning literature [1-5]. The network weights of each epoch can be regarded as realizations of such random variable. By modeling neural network weights as a multivariate random variable $\bf{W}$, the analysis of generalization can be well accommendated by the PAC-Bayesian framework e.g., in [1][2][3], where the weights are modeled as a multivariate random variable as well. As a matter of fact, we clearly stated many times in our submission, and we do not think it could cause any confusion. For instance, the "weight covariance matrix" mentioned in Abstract and Introduction; "second-order statistics of weight vectors when treated as a multivariate random variable" in Introduction; specifically in section 3.1 that we specifically model weights as a non-spherical Gaussian random variable $\bf{W}$ with mean $vec(W^F)$; in Section 4, we state that $W^F$ also can be seen as a MAP estimate of weights, so we can use Laplace approximation to estimate the covariance matrix of $\bf{W}$ [6].

**Q: Similarly, I guess that the visualization of Figures 1(b)(d) are obtained with t-SNE, but it needs to be stated.**
   
**A:** In the caption of Figure 1, we mention that "the details of .... in Appendix A". In Appendix A, we have provided the structure of the network and stated that 'We visualize the features of Dense-2 layer in Figure 1.' **Note that it's a Dense-2 layer, so we can visualize it directly.**

**Q: the revised version claims that Langford & Shawe-Taylor treat the weight as deterministic variables, which is disputable as they consider (prior and posterior) distributions over weights...** 

**A:** Thank the reviewer for pointing out this possible confusion. We meant that,  'weight volume is a property of the weight covariance matrix, while weight vector norm is a property directly over weights'. This will be clarified in the new version.

If the reviewer has further questions, please let us know.

spectrally-normalized margin bounds for neural networks. ICLR, 2018a.

deep (stochastic) neural networks with many more parameters than training data. UAI, 2017.

content.title: Re: Reply to the Feedback.
content.comment:
I agree that neural network weights can be modeled as random variables (as any machine learning model parameters!). The question is: How do we define the random distribution? There is plenty of ways to do so! One could think of many sources of randomness in the training process of a neural network (random initialization, dropout, SGD - including random mini-batches ordering, etc). My comprehension is that the random weights considered by the authors take values that lie in the same local minima as the parameters obtained by the optimization process. Please correct me if I missed it, but I do not think this is rigorously stated in the manuscript. **I would also be happy to hear what other reviewers think about this!**

Regarding the visualization, I was unfamiliar with the term *Dense-N layer* to define a *fully connected layer with N hidden units*, but it might be common among ICLR community. I thank the authors for the explanation (I actually like this visualization a lot!)

Sampling method and Laplace approximation implicitly suggest that random weights lie in the same local minima, but we think this implicit condition is obvious [1-3] as we are working with well-trained DNN (i.e., trained until converge) (e.g., for Laplace approximation, $W^F$ can be seen as a MAP estimate of weights). It is a common implicit condition in recent works (ref Footnote) and can be easily clarified by including 1-2 sentences into the paper.

Thanks very much for pointing it out, for the convenience of the reader, we are happy to make this explicit in the next version.

If the reviewer has further questions, please let us know.

* Last but not least, it can be a significant topic to study whether the weight volume -- when combined with the PAC-Bayesian adversarial generalization bound [27] -- can provide any guidance to the hot topic of adversarial generalization. 

**Q5: Other comments:**

**4.Table 2 results: The generalization gap (GG) metric needs to be properly defined in the main paper, notably the purpose of . It is crucial to interpret the results.**

content.title: Reply to the Reviewer wW51 (Part 2/4)
content.comment:
**A2:**  We really appreciate these valuable comments and the list of references on the early works of PAC-Bayes. Following your suggestion, in the updated version, we have included more discussions in Section 6 (Related Work). For your convenience, the added paragraph is as below: 

Since the invention of the PAC-Bayesian framework [1], there have been a number of canonical works developed in the past decades, including the parametrization of the PAC-Bayesian bound with Gaussian distribution [2,3,4], the early works about generalization error bounds for learning problems [5-8] and the recent works about PAC-Bayes for machine learning models [9-20]. 
Specifically, [4,6,7] demonstrate that one can obtain tight PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds through multiplying the weight vector norm with a constant,  this is different with the idea of expanding weight volume,  as weight volume is a  statistical property of weight matrices treated as random variables, while weight vector norm treats weights as deterministic variables (weight vector norm can be seen as the first term in Eq. (5), while weight volume is the second term).  It is interesting that [15] also optimizes PAC-Bayesian bound through a Gaussian posterior with a full covariance matrix.  We use a similar assumption (correlated Gaussian posterior) but the main differences are: we develop it under another PAC-Bayesian branch [21,22,23] and apply it on DNNs with connection to dropout noise.

**Q3: (3) Beginning with the abstract, the text mentions several times that "weight expansion should be regarded as the cause for the increased generalization capacity". This seems an (enthusiastic) overstatement, as the paper shows a correlation more than causality, and the supplementary material shows that other common regularizers - weight decay and batch normalization - do not tend to increase the weight expansion (this is elusively mentioned in the paper). While the paper presents an extensive empirical study exhibiting a link between weight expansion and generalization, it does not explain the mechanisms linking both phenomena. Intuitively, I would guess that the weight expansion metric captures a notion of margin or predictive stability, the latter being the cause of generalization. Similarly, explaining the SVM, I would not say that promoting a small weight vector norm is the cause of its generalization ability; however, a small vector norm translates into a large classification margin, which improves generalization.**

**A3:** Thanks for the discussion. Actually, our argument on the 'cause' is elicited from the two hypotheses we made in the Introduction, i.e., weight expansion reduces the generalization error and the dropout leads to weight expansion, respectively. In the paper, we present theoretical findings and empirical evidence to justify these hypotheses. After seeing your comment, we realized that the wording ``cause'' can be controversial, and may be seen as too enthusiastic. Therefore, we have attempted to tune down the tone of the wording as below. In the meantime, we would really appreciate if you have further advice on this.

1. **Page 1 Abstract:** $\quad$ weight expansion should be regarded as the cause for the increased generalization capacity obtained by using dropout $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$
 weight expansion can be regarded as an indicator of the enhanced generalization capability endowed by dropout

2. **Page 1 Hypothesis (1):** $\quad$ weight expansion is one of the keys $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$ weight expansion reduces the generalization error 

3. **Page 2 Section 1 Last paragraph:** $\quad$ weight expansion is a cause of a reduced generalization error $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$ weight expansion is a key indicator for a reduced generalization error

4. **Page 9 Section 5 Last paragraph:** $\quad$ serves as a key attribute of good generalization performance $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$  can serve as a key indicator of good generalization performance

5. **Page 9 Conclusion:** $\quad$ which show
that weight expansion is one of the keys to reduce the generalization error $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$ which show that weight expansion can be one of the key indicators of the reduced generalization error

We recognize that finding the essential reason for generalization is a difficult task, which we are working hard for, and weight volume may be a key indicator to further explore the generalization.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors study the generalization error through the notion of weight expansion. It is shown that a weight expansion reduces the generalization error and that dropout is an efficient method that increases the weight volume. Authors also argue that weight expansion should be regarded as the cause of better generalization.
content.main_review:
Strengths
* The manuscript is mostly well written. The arguments made by the authors are stated clearly.
* Introduce a new concept (weight expansion) to characterize generalization error.
* Provide experiments to support the technical claims.
* The weight expansion concept could open new questions worth studying.

Weaknesses
* Minor: Proofs are based on well-known techniques so there is not much novelty in this case.
* Major: Authors claim that "weight expansion should be regarded as the cause for the increased generalization capacity" but there is no formal proof of this in the paper.
* Moderate: Lack of discussion about the effect of weight expansion on the error upper bound.
content.summary_of_the_review:
After my first read of the paper, I am recommending weak acceptance. It would help if the authors can comment on my following concerns:

1. Authors have shown "relationships" between weight expansion and generalization error. However, what is been shown is not a formal proof of causality, which is an overstating of the contributions. Related to this I have two questions:
    * In the equation right before eq.(5), we have in the numerator of $\ln$ the product of the diagonal entries of the covariance matrix from the prior $P$, not $Q$! Thus, that is not precisely the weight volume according to the definition of weight expansion in Def 3.1. Either this is a mistake, which would badly hurt the paper, or there is an implicit assumption that could also hurt the contributions depending on how strong that is.
    * Authors disregard other terms regarding the weights. In eq.(5), the volume is not the only quantity that changes. Why is the norm not being considered? How do we know that perhaps that plays a more critical role?

2. Can authors comment on the numerical effect of a larger weight volume? For instance, it looks like if another method could double the weight volume the numerical value in the error upper bound could be not really significant.

content.comment:
This is mainly because the non-spherical Gaussian assumption, which allows arbitrary covariance between different directions while retaining the $\sigma^2$ variation in every direction. Essentially, this assumption is equivalent to $\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_P^\{-1\}\Sigma_Q)=k$ and $\prod_i [\Sigma_\{l,P\}]_\{ii\}=\prod_i [\Sigma_\{l,Q\}]_\{ii\}$ for all $l$. (we have attempted to make this assumption more clear in the updated manuscript of Page 4 above Eq. (5) )

We would also like to discuss the rationale of our assumption. First of all, it is a relaxation from the spherical Gaussian assumption that is used in a lot of recent PAC-Bayesian literature for DNNs, including e.g., works for PAC-Bayesian theory [1,2,3,4], and works for PAC-Bayesian bound in complexity measures [5,6,7]. Second, we note that, even the original spherical Gaussian assumption has its rationales. In Eq. (3), the inequality holds for all potential prior $P$ and posterior $Q$. That is, we are free to assume specific priors to compute the bound, and we can manually set a prior value to compute the bound. Under this circumstance, it is not hard to see that, when computing the bound, letting $\sigma_P=\sigma_Q$ is a more reasonable choice than setting $\sigma_{P}$ as a random positive number.  

**Q4: Moderate: Lack of discussion about the effect of weight expansion on the error upper bound.**

**Authors disregard other terms regarding the weights. In eq.(5), the volume is not the only quantity that changes. Why is the norm not being considered? How do we know that perhaps that plays a more critical role?**

**A4:** Actually, there are many works that study the first term in Eq. (5), see e.g., [1-7], which think the first term (e.g., spectral norm, Frobenius norm, orthogonality) is also correlated with generalization. In this paper, we introduce the second term into Eq. (5) and study the relation between the second term and dropout with an assumption that the first term remains stable with/without dropout.

The above assumption doesn't come from nowhere. Actually, it has theoretical support from Section 3.2 that the current dropout re-scales the non-drop nodes with coefficient $\frac{1}{1-q}$, which helps to keep the same output expectation (compare with no dropout). This re-scale also helps to keep the same expectation of gradient updates, further to stabilize the scale of weights (with/without dropout). Moreover, our experiments in section 5.2 indicate that, in dropout networks, the single first term (PAC-Sharpness) only gets a poor performance as bad as other normal complexity measures, but the second term (PAC-S(Laplace),PAC-S(Sampling)) can improve the performance a lot compared with the single first term (PAC-Sharpness). 

**Q5: Can authors comment on the numerical effect of a larger weight volume? For instance, it looks like if another method could double the weight volume the numerical value in the error upper bound could be not really significant.**

**A5:**

1. First, we acknowledge that the value of weight volume can indicate the trend of generalization, but may not be used to accurately predict the value (or value change) of the generalization gap, which is a very challenging task and there exists no miracle solution till now [6].

2. Second, according to Equation (5), doubling the weight volume will reduce the KL divergence $D_{KL}(Q_l||P_l)$ by a constant $\frac{\ln 2}{2}$ in each layer. While it might be hard to judge the significance of this number from the Equation, in Section 5.3, we show empirically that this change can have a significant impact on the generalization error of the network; and in Section 5.2, we demonstrate that capturing this change of weight volume can improve the performance of complexity measure for dropout networks.

[4] Liao, Renjie, Raquel Urtasun, and Richard Zemel. "A PAC-Bayesian Approach to Generalization Bounds for Graph Neural Networks." ICLR. 2020.

[5] Yiding Jiang, Behnam Neyshabur, Hossein Mobahi, Dilip Krishnan, and Samy Bengio.  Fantasticgeneralization measures and where to find them. ICLR, 2020.

[6] Karolina Gintare Dziugaite, Alexandre Drouin, Brady Neal, Nitarshan Rajkumar, Ethan Caballero,Linbo Wang, Ioannis Mitliagkas, and Daniel Roy. In search of robust measures of generalization. NeurIPS, 2020.

[7] Chatterji, N. S., Neyshabur, B., and Sedghi, H. The intriguing role of module criticality in thegeneralization of deep networks. ICLR, 2020.

content.title: Reply to the Reviewer iaGH (Part 1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed and positive feedback, our responses to the reviewer’s specific questions are below:

**Q1: Minor: Proofs are based on well-known techniques so there is not much novelty in this case.**

**A1:** As mentioned in the paper, a key technical novelty is to relax a critical assumption in the PAC-Bayesian framework
from the spherical to non-spherical Gaussian posterior, from which the generalization ability is related to the new measure of weight volume. Further, Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 demonstrate how dropout expands weight volume through the reduced correlation of updated gradients and weights. In doing so, the relation between generalization and dropout is established. Although the proofs are not necessarily new or complex, we believe the connection between generalization and dropout is insightful and totally non-trivial, see Appendix D, E, and F. It is worth noting that these lemmas do not stand alone -- they are important ingredients of our main contribution, i.e., a framework for explaining the generalization of dropout through the lens of weight volume.

**Q2: Authors claim that ‘weight expansion should be regarded as the cause for the increased generalization capacity’ but there is no formal proof of this in the paper.**
 
**Authors have shown ‘relationships’ between weight expansion and generalization error. However, what is been shown is not a formal proof of causality, which is an overstating of the contributions.**

**A2:** Our argument regarding the relation between weight volume and the generalization gap is formally stated with the two hypotheses at the beginning of the Introduction: weight expansion reduces the generalization error, and the dropout leads to weight expansion. These hypotheses are then validated with both theoretical arguments (updating PAC-Bayesian framework to include weight volume) and many experimental results, in particular we show that the increase of weight volume leads to improved generalization ability and the decrease of weight volume leads to reduced generalization ability. We termed such relation as a causality relation in the original manuscript. But after receiving your and (the other reviewer's) comments, we realized that this wording can be misleading, and have attempted to revise it in the updated manuscript. Below are a few places we have updated. 

1. **Page 1 Abstract:** $\quad$ weight expansion should be regarded as the cause for the increased generalization capacity obtained by using dropout $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$
 weight expansion can be regarded as an indicator of the enhanced generalization capability endowed by dropout

2. **Page 1 Hypothesis (1):** $\quad$ weight expansion is one of the keys $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$ weight expansion reduces the generalization error 

3. **Page 2 Section 1 Last paragraph:** $\quad$ weight expansion is a cause of a reduced generalization error $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$ weight expansion is a key indicator for a reduced generalization error

4. **Page 9 Section 5 Last paragraph:** $\quad$ serves as a key attribute of good generalization performance $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$  can serve as a key indicator of good generalization performance

5. **Page 9 Conclusion:** $\quad$ which show
that weight expansion is one of the keys to reduce the generalization error $\quad \longrightarrow \quad$ which show that weight expansion can be one of the key indicators of the reduced generalization error

**Q3: In the equation right before eq.(5), we have in the numerator of the ln product of the diagonal entries of the covariance matrix from the prior P, not Q! Thus, that is not precisely the weight volume according to the definition of weight expansion in Def 3.1. Either this is a mistake, which would badly hurt the paper, or there is an implicit assumption that could also hurt the contributions depending on how strong that is.**

**A3:** In Eq. (5), we relax their assumption by letting $Q$ be a non-spherical Gaussian (but still with the same variance $\sigma^2$ as same as their assumption). Thus, the whole derivation of Eq. (5) should be
\begin{align}
D_\{KL\}(Q||P)&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_l \Big( \frac{||W_l^F-W_l^0||_F^2}{\sigma_l^2} + \ln{\frac{\prod_i [\Sigma_\{l,P\}]_\{ii\}}{\det(\Sigma_\{l,Q\})}}\Big) \\\\
&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_l \Big( \frac{||W_l^F-W_l^0||_F^2}{\sigma_l^2} + \ln{\frac{\prod_i [\Sigma_\{l,Q\}]_\{ii\}}{\det(\Sigma_\{l,Q\})}}\Big) \\\\
&=\frac{1}{2} \sum_l \Big( \frac{||W_l^F-W_l^0||_F^2}{\sigma_l^2} +\ln{\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(\bf{W}_l)}}\Big).
\end{align}
Note that, from first line of above equation to the second line, we replace $\prod_i [\Sigma_\{l,P\}]_\{ii\}$ with $\prod_i [\Sigma_\{l,Q\}]_\{ii\}$ because they are equivalent under our assumption.
